nodes.name: Data & Security System
nodes.note: Useful systems must represent data accurately while controlling who can read, change or disrupt it.
nodes.hook: Take one college system and map both its data model and its security risks.

nodes.name: Structured Data
nodes.note: Structured data uses consistent fields, types and relationships so information can be stored, validated and queried predictably.
nodes.hook: Turn an unstructured sign-up form response into fields with explicit data types.

nodes.name: Table
nodes.note: A relational table stores rows that share a defined set of columns and constraints.
nodes.hook: Explain why one huge table is often harder to maintain than several related tables.

nodes.name: Field / Column
nodes.note: A field represents one attribute with a defined meaning and data type.
nodes.hook: Choose a data type that prevents an impossible value rather than storing everything as text.

nodes.name: Record / Row
nodes.note: A record groups values describing one instance represented by the table.
nodes.hook: Identify what one row means in three different tables from the same system.

nodes.name: Primary Key
nodes.note: A primary key uniquely identifies each record and provides a stable target for relationships.
nodes.hook: Explain why a person's display name is usually a poor primary key.

nodes.name: Foreign Key
nodes.note: A foreign key stores a reference to a key in another table, representing a relationship while supporting referential integrity.
nodes.hook: Show how one team can reference many players without copying the team name into every design decision.

nodes.name: Relationships
nodes.note: Relationships describe how records in different tables correspond, such as one-to-many or many-to-many associations.
nodes.hook: Model students and esports teams, then decide whether membership needs a junction table.

nodes.name: Normalisation
nodes.note: Normalisation restructures relational data to reduce avoidable duplication and update anomalies while preserving meaningful relationships.
nodes.hook: Find one repeated fact that could become inconsistent if it is updated in only one place.

nodes.name: Validation & Constraints
nodes.note: Validation and constraints reject data that violates defined rules, types, ranges or relationships.
nodes.hook: Distinguish validation from verification using a student ID example.

nodes.name: SQL Operations
nodes.note: SQL provides declarative operations for selecting, combining, aggregating and changing relational data.
nodes.hook: Describe the result you want before thinking about the exact SQL syntax.

nodes.name: SELECT
nodes.note: SELECT retrieves rows and expressions from one or more data sources according to query clauses.
nodes.hook: Write a question in plain English, then identify which fields and rows the query must return.

nodes.name: Filtering
nodes.note: Filtering limits result rows according to conditions, commonly using WHERE predicates.
nodes.hook: Explain the difference between filtering source rows and sorting the final result.

nodes.name: JOIN
nodes.note: JOIN combines related rows from multiple sources according to a matching condition.
nodes.hook: Draw the relationship before writing the join so you know which keys should match.

nodes.name: Aggregation & GROUP BY
nodes.note: Aggregation summarises groups of rows using operations such as count, sum, average, minimum or maximum.
nodes.hook: Turn individual match records into one statistic per player without losing sight of what the statistic hides.

nodes.name: INSERT / UPDATE / DELETE
nodes.note: Data-modification statements create, change or remove persistent records and therefore require careful validation and permissions.
nodes.hook: Explain why a missing WHERE clause can turn a small update into a major incident.

nodes.name: Database Index
nodes.note: Indexes provide alternative access paths that can speed suitable queries while consuming storage and adding maintenance cost to writes.
nodes.hook: Explain why indexing every column is not automatically good database design.

nodes.name: Cybersecurity Risk
nodes.note: Cybersecurity manages risk to systems, services and information by understanding assets, threats, vulnerabilities, impact and controls.
nodes.hook: Use one real system to distinguish threat, vulnerability and impact without treating them as synonyms.

nodes.name: Asset
nodes.note: An asset is something valuable that needs protection, such as data, identity, service availability, hardware or reputation.
nodes.hook: List assets before listing attacks so the security discussion stays tied to actual value.

nodes.name: Threat
nodes.note: A threat is a circumstance or actor capable of causing harm to an asset.
nodes.hook: Separate a malicious actor from the vulnerability they might exploit.

nodes.name: Vulnerability
nodes.note: A vulnerability is a weakness that can be exploited or triggered to cause unwanted impact.
nodes.hook: Explain why an exposed admin page is not automatically a successful attack.

nodes.name: Risk
nodes.note: Risk considers the possibility and consequence of harm so controls can be prioritised rather than applied blindly.
nodes.hook: Compare two vulnerabilities and justify which should be fixed first using impact and likelihood.

nodes.name: Confidentiality, Integrity & Availability
nodes.note: The CIA model distinguishes protection from unauthorised disclosure, unauthorised or incorrect change, and loss of access to needed services or data.
nodes.hook: Classify three incidents by which security property is primarily harmed.

nodes.name: Identity, Authentication & Authorisation
nodes.note: Identity controls establish who or what is requesting access and what actions that identity is allowed to perform.
nodes.hook: Explain why successfully logging in does not mean a user should be allowed to do everything.

nodes.name: Authentication
nodes.note: Authentication verifies a claimed identity using one or more factors or credentials.
nodes.hook: Compare password-only authentication with MFA in terms of what an attacker must obtain.

nodes.name: Authorisation & Access Control
nodes.note: Authorisation determines whether an authenticated identity may perform a requested action on a resource.
nodes.hook: Test an application by asking what happens when a normal user changes an ID in a URL or request.

nodes.name: Role-Based Access Control
nodes.note: RBAC assigns permissions to roles and users to roles so access can be managed around job responsibilities rather than individually everywhere.
nodes.hook: Design roles for student, teacher and administrator without giving all staff administrator rights.

nodes.name: Cryptographic Protection
nodes.note: Cryptographic controls protect data or credentials through mechanisms such as encryption, hashing and authenticated secure channels.
nodes.hook: Choose hashing or encryption for a stored password and explain why they solve different problems.

nodes.name: Password Hashing
nodes.note: Password systems should store one-way password verifiers rather than recoverable plaintext passwords.
nodes.hook: Explain why encrypting passwords with a reversible key creates a different risk from password hashing.

nodes.name: Encryption
nodes.note: Encryption transforms data so that authorised parties with suitable keys can recover the original information while others cannot practically read it.
nodes.hook: Distinguish data at rest from data in transit when selecting a control.

nodes.name: Secure Input & Injection Prevention
nodes.note: Applications must treat external input as untrusted data and keep it separate from commands, queries or code interpretation.
nodes.hook: Explain why a database query built by string concatenation can turn user data into query syntax.

nodes.name: Parameterized Queries
nodes.note: Parameterized queries keep values separate from SQL syntax so user-controlled input is not interpreted as part of the command structure.
nodes.hook: Compare a concatenated query with a parameterized query and identify where interpretation changes.

nodes.name: Software Supply Chain
nodes.note: Applications inherit risk from dependencies, build tools, packages and delivery systems as well as from first-party code.
nodes.hook: List what must be trusted when a project installs a package from a public registry.
